Hello, my name is Sweety Kumari Vishwakarma. In this recording I present my solution to the assignment on the paper by Álvarez Roa and co-authors, 'A simplified FSO channel model with weak turbulence and pointing errors', from ICTON 2024. I will go through the five tasks in order: first the model and why the composite PDF is numerically unstable, then my reproduction of Figure 2, then a check of the approximation, then the stretch task, where I chose option (b), the outage probability, and finally the follow-up that I propose. All results come from my own Python code, which I am sending together with this video. The three coloured dots you will see throughout are the three operating points of Figure 2: green with small pointing error and the strongest turbulence, yellow in the middle, and pink with the largest pointing error and the weakest turbulence. [about 45 s]

The system is intensity modulation with direct detection and on-off keying. Bits are mapped to zero or 2P, pass through the channel, get Gaussian noise added, and the receiver, which knows h, compares y with the midpoint eta h P. The channel gain is the product of three independent losses. h-l is the Beer-Lambert atmospheric loss. It depends on the weather and changes over minutes to hours, so over the analysis window it is deterministic: 0.2208 dB per km over 3 km gives 0.859. h-p is geometric spread plus pointing error. The beam has spread to almost 2 metres at the receiver while the aperture radius is 5 cm, so even with perfect alignment only 1.27 times 10 to the minus 3 of the power is collected; that is A-zero. The beam centre jitters with Gaussian x and y displacements, so the radial offset is Rayleigh. Pushed through the Gaussian collection formula, eq. (6), the quantity V = 2R squared over w-z-eq squared is exponential with rate gamma squared, and h-p over A-zero equals e to the minus V. That gives eq. (7) directly. h-a is turbulence. In the Rytov picture the log-amplitude chi is a sum of many small perturbations, hence Gaussian; the irradiance is e to the 2 chi, and requiring a mean of one fixes the mean of chi to minus sigma-X squared. That is eq. (5), with sigma-X squared equal to a quarter of the Rytov variance. [about 1 min 45 s]

The step that made everything else simple for me is this change of variable. If I take the logarithm of h normalised by A-zero h-l, the product becomes a sum: a Gaussian from turbulence minus an exponential from the pointing error. After standardising the Gaussian, z equals W minus E-prime, where W is standard normal and E-prime is exponential with rate kappa, and kappa is gamma squared times sigma-R. This is the exponentially modified Gaussian distribution. Eq. (10) of the paper is exactly kappa times e to the kappa z plus kappa squared over 2, times Q of z plus kappa. And if I insert the approximation (13) and merge the exponents, the paper's eq. (14) collapses to the Gaussian phi of z divided by 1 plus z over kappa, for z larger than minus kappa. So eq. (14) is the log-normal turbulence PDF times a correction for the pointing error. The plots show Monte Carlo samples, generated from the physics and not from the PDFs, against both. For kappa 68 and 11 the two curves are on top of each other; for kappa 2.5, the pink point, the approximation overshoots and has a spike at z equal to minus kappa, which is h-hat. Keep kappa in mind; it controls everything that follows. [about 1 min 30 s]

Why does eq. (10) fail for small pointing errors? Written as in the paper, it is a product of four factors. At the green point gamma squared is 68, and the factors are about e to the 2353, e to the 465, e to the minus 458 and e to the minus 2319. The product is a perfectly normal number, but double precision can only hold e to the minus 745 up to e to the 709. So exp returns infinity, erfc returns zero, and infinity times zero is NaN. The exponent grows like kappa squared over 2, so small sigma-s, which means large gamma, makes it worse, and so does stronger turbulence. On the right I reproduced the left panel of Figure 2: the red region is where a literal implementation of eq. (10) fails, the dashed line is the analytic overflow boundary, and the grey curves are contours of constant kappa. The fix is algebraic, not numerical: add the exponents first and use a log-Q routine, here scipy's log-n-d-t-r. Then eq. (10) is exact and stable for every operating point, and I no longer need an approximation just to evaluate the PDF. [about 1 min 20 s]

This is my reproduction of the right panel of Figure 2. Solid lines are the exact average BER, eq. (16), evaluated stably; dashed is the approximation (17); dotted is (18); circles are a bit-level Monte Carlo of the system in Figure 1 with 4 million bits per point. I draw a new channel gain for every bit, which is what the infinite interleaver means, and I detect with the threshold eta h P. The Monte Carlo agrees with the exact curve within 2.7 standard errors at 40 of 41 powers; the one outlier I re-ran with other seeds and it fell within one sigma. At the HD-FEC limit I get delta of 0.0004 dB for green and 0.018 dB for yellow, against 0 and 0.02 in the paper, and for (18) 0.75 and 0.44 dB, against about 0.7 and 0.4. Across all nine operating points of the left panel, eight agree with the paper to within 0.015 dB. The exception is pink, where I get 1.3 dB instead of 0.18. The next slide explains why. [about 1 min 15 s]

Here are the two cases that I think are the most interesting. On the left, the green point. The paper says eq. (16) cannot be evaluated there and shows only Monte Carlo. I confirm that: coded literally with scipy's quad, the integral returns NaN at every power. But with the log-domain form the exact BER is finite and passes through all the Monte Carlo points. On the right, the pink point. The approximate PDF (14) contains one over z plus kappa, which comes from the erfc approximation e to the minus x squared over x root pi; it blows up at x equal to zero, that is at h-hat. One over x is not integrable, so the area under (14) and the integral (17) diverge logarithmically. If I start the integral 10 to the minus 6 above h-hat I get 1.30 dB; if I start 0.1 above, I get 0.21 dB, close to the paper's 0.18. So the pink delta is not a well-defined number; it depends on where the numerical routine stops. The divergent part also decays more slowly with power than the true BER, which explains the wrong slope the paper reports for high pointing errors. [about 1 min 20 s]

Task 3 asks for the area under (14) at the nine operating points. On the left I plot the area as the lower limit approaches h-hat. For eight points the area does not depend on the limit and is slightly above one: 1.0002 for green, 1.008 for yellow, 1.047 at the worst of them. It follows the series 1 plus 1 over kappa squared plus 3 over kappa to the fourth, which comes from expanding 1 over 1 plus z over kappa under the Gaussian. For pink the area keeps growing like kappa phi of kappa times log of 1 over delta, and 2.6 percent of the true probability, below h-hat, is thrown away. The extra area sits at low h, in the deep fades that dominate the BER, so the area excess and delta move together. On the right, delta against kappa: one number organises all nine points. Why does the approximation improve with more turbulence and smaller pointing errors? Both increase kappa. The erfc argument over the bulk of the distribution is about kappa over root 2, so the relative error of (13) is about one over kappa squared: 2 times 10 to the minus 4 for green, 16 percent for pink. Physically, one over kappa is the mean pointing fade measured in units of the turbulence spread; when it is small the channel is nearly log-normal and (14) becomes exact. As a check, replacing (13) with a bounded Q approximation, Börjesson-Sundberg, removes the pole and gives a delta below 0.004 dB at all nine points, including pink. [about 1 min 45 s]

For the stretch task I chose option (b). The fading coherence time is a few milliseconds. At 10 gigabaud one fade lasts 10 to 50 million symbols, while hard-decision FEC codewords are 10 to the 4 to 10 to the 6 bits. So every codeword sees a single value of h, and the infinite interleaver would need hundreds of milliseconds of latency. The relevant quantity is then the outage probability, the probability that the conditional BER of eq. (15) exceeds the HD-FEC limit. Because the BER decreases with h, this is just the probability that h is below a threshold, and with the exponentially modified Gaussian it is closed form, the formula shown here. I checked it against a block-fading Monte Carlo. The solid curves are outage, the dashed ones the average BER. To reach an outage of 10 to the minus 3 the link needs 6.9 dB more power than the average-BER design for green, 5.5 for yellow and 3.6 for pink; for 10 to the minus 6 it is 7 to 14 dB. A coded system cares about outage, because the decoder succeeds or fails per codeword; the average BER mixes good blocks with rare deep fades where the BER is close to one half, which no FEC can repair. [about 1 min 30 s]

This leads to the follow-up I propose, and it is the part I find most worth doing. Real links are neither at N equal to 1 nor at infinite interleaving. So I propose to compute, for this channel, the power needed for a target codeword-failure probability as a function of the interleaver depth N, the number of independent fades per codeword, which is the same as latency N times T-c. A first Monte Carlo result is in the plot, and it is not what I expected. For N below about 130, interleaving does not help, and for green it even costs almost 1 dB, because one block with BER near one half is enough to push the codeword average above 3.84 times 10 to the minus 3, and more blocks give more chances to hit one. Even at N equal to 1024, about one second at 1 ms coherence, green is still 1.1 dB away from the infinite-interleaver answer. Why does it matter? This is the number a designer of an FSO or satellite link with a latency budget actually needs. It is tractable, because with the exponentially modified Gaussian the N equal 1 case is closed form and for larger N a Chernoff bound with the moment generating function shown here gives a design chart in kappa and N. And it points to a better receiver: since the receiver knows h, it could erase deeply faded blocks and let an outer erasure code recover them, and this framework can measure that gain. [about 1 min 40 s]

To summarise. In the log domain the channel is a Gaussian minus an exponential, with one parameter kappa equal to gamma squared sigma-R. Eq. (10) fails as infinity times zero, but in log form it is exact everywhere and agrees with Monte Carlo, including at the green point. I reproduced Figure 2; eight of the nine deltas match the paper within 0.015 dB, and for the pink point I showed that (17) diverges at h-hat, so its delta depends on the integration limit. The approximation improves with kappa, and a bounded Q function fixes it everywhere. Finally, for a coded link without very deep interleaving, outage is the right metric; it is closed form for this model and needs 3.6 to 6.9 dB more power than the average-BER design, which motivates the finite-interleaver analysis I proposed. The code runs with a single command, python run_all.py, and reproduces every number and figure in this talk. Thank you for your time; I look forward to discussing it. [about 1 min]
